summary.title: How Complex Systems Fail
summary.one_liner: Complex systems are intrinsically hazardous and run in degraded mode, so failures usually come from combinations of latent faults rather than a single root cause.
keywords: new technology introduces new failure modes
richard cook how complex systems fail
takeaways: Catastrophic failure in complex systems needs several small, individually insufficient faults to line up, so there is rarely one root cause.
Systems run in degraded mode; prior proto-accidents are common and are usually visible only in hindsight.
Hindsight bias and blaming 'human error' distort post-accident analysis and can increase system complexity.
Practitioners both produce output and defend against failure, and their actions are gambles under uncertainty.
Safety is an emergent property of the whole system, created continuously by people adapting to changing conditions, and it requires experience with failure.
summary.summary: Richard Cook (University of Chicago, Cognitive Technologies Laboratory) presents 18 numbered propositions on why complex systems such as healthcare, transportation and power generation fail. Each point is short and argued in prose, with references to his and colleagues' patient-safety and human-error papers at the end. The core argument is that overt accidents need multiple latent faults combined, so attributing them to a single root cause or to individual error is wrong, especially given hindsight bias. The text also covers practitioners as adaptive defenders, the introduction of new failure modes with technology, and safety as a dynamic property of the system.
